newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Krupp-Thyssen deal could bypass takeover code.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Krupp-Thyssen deal could bypass takeover code.

text.p: Any takeover by German metals and engineering group Hoesch-Krupp of its larger steel rival Thyssen AG is likely to bypass Germany's fledgling takeover code, analysts said on Tuesday.
Krupp confirmed on Tuesday that it planned to take over Thyssen but the voluntary code set up in 1995 is just that -- a set of rules that companies can choose to follow or to ignore.

Krupp itself, formed by a rare German hostile takeover in 1991, is among the two thirds of listed firms that do not recognise the code. Therefore if it does launch a bid, its next step would not be clearly laid out.

"I think that ideally Krupp would like 100 percent of Thyssen," said Markus Reichle, German equity analyst at Paribas in London. "But even if it got 25 percent it could exert enough passive influence on Thyssen that eventually a fully-fledged merger would in any case be likely."

The well-established British takeover code, for example, would make such a waiting game unlikely. Above a 30 percent threshold, a predator is obliged to launch a full bid for all the remaining shares immediately.

But Germany's takeover code -- designed mainly to steer friendly takeovers to their conclusion -- requires a full bid only after a threshold of 50 percent. Even then a company has up to 21 months to make its offer.

There are also no compulsory purchase regulations to "mop up" remaining shares at the end of a bid, meaning that a bidder can find itself with a majority stake but with a legacy of existing small shareholders to deal with.
The lack of a clear takeover mechanism was one of the many hurdles Italy's Pirelli SpA faced in its unsuccessful attempt to acquire German tyre maker Continental AG in 1991.

In a market dominated by powerful banks and a network of cross-shareholdings, unwelcome foreign predators have had to pick their way through a minefield of takeover defences, notably restrictions on voting rights.
The sheer size of Germany's "Mittelstand", the legion of small-to-medium private companies that make up the country's economic backbone, also leaves few sizeable listed takeover targets.
Reichle said that such obstacles were gradually falling away and in any case probably figured in the calculations of industrial veteran Gerhard Cromme, Krupp's chief executive.
"This bid is a complete change of pace for Germany and I cannot imagine that Cromme would have gone into it without having fully considered the consequences," he said.
Deutsche Bank management board member Rolf Breuer said the offer showed German industry was entering a phase of stronger concentration ahead of European monetary union.

Breuer, who will take over as chief executive at Deutsche in May, said he was very interested in the Thyssen takeover proceeding in an orderly fashion like takeovers in Britain and the United States, where such deals are common.

"I very much want this first large case in Germany to proceed in an orderly fashion and hope that it demonstrates that the German financial centre is also in a position to carry out a takeover in a manner that is common in other countries," he said at a news conference on asset management.
Breuer noted that the Krupp bid was "extraordinary" by German standards in terms of its volume, participants and economic background.

Deutsche Morgan Grenfell is among three investment banks who are advising Krupp on its bid for Thyssen. Deutsche, Dresdner Bank AG and Goldman Sachs and other banks are securing financing for the deal.

Ralf Conen, a stategist at Salomon Brothers in Frankfurt, agreed the bid looked right as the corporate scene changes. "It is clearly going in the right direction. Cross-holdings are being run down and even voting right restrictions are being done away with by some companies," he said.

Even the intervention of German cartel authorities -- whose veto has repeatedly blocked construction group Hochtief AG in its attempts to gain control of Philipp Holzmann -- need not pose a threat to Krupp's ambitions, he added.
